analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice cases at $250,000 and limits punitive damages and lawyer fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on July 25, 2002 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten medical malpractice rules nationwide. It keeps unlimited recovery for out-of-pocket losses like medical bills and lost wages, but caps compensation for pain, suffering, and disfigurement at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury. It makes punitive damages much harder to win — and blocks them entirely against drug or device makers whose product was approved by the FDA — limits how much patients' lawyers can be paid, shortens the deadlines for suing, and overrides state laws that give injured patients more rights. The bill's stated goal was to lower malpractice insurance premiums and reduce 'defensive medicine' so care stays affordable and available.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians and hospitals facing malpractice premiums, malpractice insurers who pay out claims, and drug and device makers who would gain a shield from punitive damages whenever the FDA approved their product. Supporters argued patients would benefit too, through lower health care costs and more available care.

how_it_helps.text: Keeps recovery of economic losses — medical bills, lost earnings, care costs — fully unlimited.

Caps noneconomic damages (pain and suffering) at $250,000 and caps lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale, which supporters said would reduce the cost and unpredictability of malpractice litigation.
Restricts punitive damages to cases proven by clear and convincing evidence of malicious intent, and bars them against makers of FDA-approved products unless they misled or bribed the FDA.
The bill's stated purpose was to reduce defensive medicine and liability insurance premiums, which it said were driving up health care costs and reducing access to care.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence, especially those whose main loss is pain and suffering rather than lost wages — children, retirees, and people who weren't working — who could no longer recover more than $250,000 no matter how catastrophic the harm. It would also override state laws that currently give patients stronger rights.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages hits hardest those with small economic losses — children, stay-at-home parents, and retirees — whose injuries can be life-shattering but whose wage losses are modest.

A suit must generally be filed within three years of the injury or one year after discovery, with a hard three-year ceiling even for injuries discovered later, which can bar claims for harm that only shows up years after treatment.

Drug and device makers would be shielded from punitive damages whenever the FDA approved their product, except in cases of knowing misrepresentation or bribery — a protection that reduces the financial deterrent to cutting corners, since FDA approval is not a guarantee of safety.
The bill preempts state law unless the state gives providers greater protection, so states that currently allow higher recoveries for injured patients would lose those rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, one-sided relief to health care providers, insurers, and drug makers by cutting the largest malpractice awards. Its promised benefit to patients — lower premiums and better access — is indirect and not guaranteed by anything in the bill, while the costs fall directly on the most severely injured patients, whose compensation is capped and whose deadlines to sue are shortened. An honest weighing finds the protections for industry are concrete and immediate while the benefits to ordinary people are speculative.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate on July 25, 2002, sent straight to the Judiciary Committee, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Senator John Ensign introduced the HEALTH Act of 2002 in the Senate on July 25, 2002, joined by five Republican cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
No further action — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote — is recorded before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients kept their existing rights under state law to sue for malpractice, while insurers, physicians, and drug makers did not get the liability limits the bill would have given them.

for.name: Sen. John Ensign
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: American Medical Association
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed Congress for federal caps on malpractice damages during the insurance premium crisis of the early 2000s.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 25, 2002 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal caps on malpractice damages and lawyer fees, which would sharply reduce recoveries for injured patients.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote was ever taken; all six senators attached to the bill were Republicans, and no Democrat publicly supported it in the record.

industries.note: Capping pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000 and restricting punitive damages directly limits the claims insurers must pay. The saving goes to insurers and policyholders rather than to injured patients.

The bill bars punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved products unless they knowingly misled or bribed the FDA. This removes a major financial deterrent in product-injury cases involving prescription drugs and devices.

Providers gain capped liability exposure and shorter deadlines for suits, which supporters said would lower premiums and keep doctors practicing. The cost is that patients harmed by negligence have less recourse against those same providers.

The bill caps contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% above $600,000) and gives courts power to redirect fee payments. Lawyers' loss of income tracks the reduction in recoveries for injured patients.

industries.industry: Health insurers and other benefit payers
industries.note: The bill lets defendants introduce evidence of collateral source benefits (like insurance payouts) to reduce awards, but bars those benefit payers from liens or reimbursement against the patient's recovery. Benefit payers lose subrogation rights while defendants gain an offset.
